531

small compared with u and w and the pressure constant in the y-direction.
This implies that changes in both the x- and z-directions are slow, compared with changes in the y-direction. Such a flow occurs, for example, on
finite wings and propeller blades, excluding the regions near the root and
tip. The flow in those regions is called slender 3D flow, and changes in the
y- and z-directions are rapid, compared with changes in the x-direction.
Some slender 3D flows develop discrete longitudinal vortices in the boundary layer. An example is the horseshoe vortex that forms in a wing-body
junction. Most of the analytical and numerical work in the literature has
dealt with boundary sheet flows.
The boundary layer approximation in 3D flow also implies some new
mathematical properties of the equation system. The 3D Navier-Stokes
equations are elliptic, which means that information from a given point in
the flow can be propagated by convection, viscous diffusion, or pressure
perturbations. In a 3D boundary layer, propagation by the pressure has
been eliminated by taking 0p/0y < 0. Also, viscous diffusion has been eliminated in the x- and z-directions. Thus, information is propagated in the
cross-flow plane only by convection at an angle tan−1 (w/u) in the plan view.
Taken all together, these properties imply that the influence of the solution
at one point is transferred to other points first by viscous diffusion along a
line across the boundary sheet through that point in the y-direction and
then by convection downstream along all streamlines through that vertical
line. This forms a zone of influence bounded by the body surface at the
bottom, the boundary sheet edge at the top, and the two characteristic surfaces normal to the surface containing the external, inviscid and wall
streamlines. This configuration is illustrated in Fig. 11.1. On the other

11.1.1

Separation of Three-Dimensional
Boundary Layers

It was mentioned earlier that a 3D flow in an adverse pressure gradient can turn laterally and avoid separation. This possibility leads to significant changes and complexity in separation patterns. In 2D flows, one
simply looks for the location of any points where ('u/'y)w 5 0, and the
flow pattern is as shown in Fig. 1.10. In 3D flows, the mathematical condition can be generalized to say that separation corresponds to ('q/'y)w
5 0, where q is the component of velocity perpendicular to the separation
line. This is much less clear from a physical point of view. Maskell
(1955) distinguishes two broad types of 3D separations, as illustrated in
Fig. 11.2. The case in Fig. 11.2a is said to form a separation bubble that
encloses fluid that is not part of the main stream, but rather is carried
along with the body. Formation of the bubble entails one singular saddle
point, denoted by S on Fig. 11.2a. The behavior of the flow at this point,
and this point alone, resembles that in a 2D separation. In the second
case, shown in Fig. 11.2b, the space on either side of the surface of separation is filled with fluid from the main stream. Maskell suggested that a
separation surface be viewed as consisting of the separating limiting
streamlines coming from upstream and downstream (reversed-flow)
regions. He argued that separation occurs when two such streamlines
meet. They then merge and leave the surface as a single separation
streamline. This is shown schematically in Fig. 11.3. In the ordinary case,
the separation streamline first is tangent to the body surface and then
lifts off, as drawn in Fig. 11.3b. For a singular separation, such as that at
point S in Fig. 11.2a, the separation streamline inclines to the body surface
immediately.

The last special case to be considered is the infinite swept wing, or, more
generally, infinite yawed cylinder. Flows over finite swept wings are of
interest in aerodynamic applications, and the case of an infinite version
allows great simplification to the equations of motion. The inviscid, external flow over an infinite swept cylinder can be found by the superposition
of two flows, one lying in planes normal to the cylinder axis and the second

Interestingly, the solution for u and υ can be found from the first two equations independently of w. Then, the last equation is linear, and it can be
solved for w using the known u and υ as coefficients. This is reminiscent of
the case for the low-speed energy equation in Sec. 4.4. Separation can occur only through the effects of an adverse pressure gradient formed by
Ue(x), not We. This whole special behavior was called the independence
principle by Prandtl (1946).
The simplest example is, as usual, a flat plate, in this case with the
leading edge yawed to the uniform approach flow. Thus, both Ue and We are
constant. The solution for u and υ is just the Blasius 2D solution, and the
equations can be seen to admit to the simple solution w/u 5 We/Ue. At each
point across the boundary layer, the resultant of u and w forms a profile
that is itself a Blasius profile. The flow is then independent of yawing of the
leading edge, and there is no streamline skewing. This kind of analysis has
been extended to Cooke’s (1950) yawed equivalent of the Falkner-Skan
wedge flows discussed in the 2D case in Sec. 4.3.2. There really is no great
practical utility to this very restrictive, special class of flows.

Integral Methods

Copyright © 2011. American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics. All rights reserved.

As with all integral methods, the main issue in 3D integral methods is
the selection of the shape(s) of the velocity profile(s). Experience with 2D
cases is helpful in selecting the shape of the profile of the streamwise velocity component. However, the choice of shape for the profile of the crossflow velocity component presents new and difficult problems. If the
streamline skewing is all in one direction for a given problem, the choice is
not so trying. But, if, as in the general case, the skewing first is in one direction and then changes direction under the influence of the inviscid pressure gradient, the crossflow profile can have a complicated S-shape. The
crossflow velocity in one part of the layer is in one direction, and that in
another part of the layer is in the opposite direction. The development or
relaxation of this behavior is obviously important in predicting the flow,
and it is hard to “build in” the correct behavior in the choice of profile.
Most workers have chosen to employ two boundary layer thicknesses to
describe the two velocity profiles. Wild (1949) proposed

for his treatment of the case of the infinite yawed wing. In that case, d is
known from the equivalent 2D solution, and D is the remaining unknown.
The latter is found from the remaining momentum equation. With the assumptions in Eq. (11.30), the w-profile is independent of the u-profile. In
other methods, especially for turbulent flows, it is common to express the
shape of the w-profile in terms of the shape of the u-profile. For the case of
an infinite swept wing, Rott and Crabtree (1952) have extended the
Thwaites-Walz 2D method described in Sec. 2.3.2.
All in all, the serious limitations of integral methods for 3D laminar
flows has resulted in their being little used in modern times. The use of
integral methods for 3D turbulent cases is more common, and we shall
consider that subject later in Sec. 11.4.4. If one needs accurate solutions for
3D laminar flows under fairly general conditions, the only choice is numerical solutions.

Only the schemes in the lower part of Fig. 11.8c are stable for reverse

The finite-difference equations for all these methods result in a system of
algebraic equations that are linearized, as in the 2D case, giving a system
that can be solved with the Thomas algorithm. The continuity equation can
again be written in finite difference form to give an explicit relation for υ as
the only unknown.
One can distinguish three broad classes of 3D boundary layer flows for
numerical treatment:
1. Tip, stagnation point, or leading edge flows. The equations are functions
of y and x3 alone. A 2D finite difference scheme is needed, and the
solution is started where the crossflow is zero.
2. Plane-of-symmetry flows. The equations are functions of y and x1 alone.
A 2D finite difference scheme is needed, and the solution is started at
the tip, stagnation point, or leading edge.
3. General 3D flows. The equations are functions of x1, y, and x3. One of the
3D finite difference schemes is needed.
Finally, just as in the 2D case, it has proven convenient to introduce
transformations that approximately scale the computational region
with the growth of the boundary layer. Numerous suggestions have
been made. To illustrate, we pick one suggestion from Dwyer and
McCroskey (1971) for constant-density, constant-property flow and
Cartesian coordinates:

11.3 Transition to Turbulent Flow

There is much less data for transition in 3D boundary layer flows than
for the corresponding 2D cases. Combined with the fact that the parameter
space for 3D cases is much larger than for 2D cases, this leads to the result
that the date base for transition in 3D flows is exceedingly sparse.
One can make some general observations about transition in 3D versus
2D boundary layer flows. In the 2D case, we saw in Chapter 6 that velocity
profiles with an inflection point were much less stable and thus were much
more prone to transition. In a 3D boundary layer, there is necessarily at
least one inflection point in the crossflow velocity profile because the
crossflow velocity must, even in the simplest cases, vary from zero at the
wall up to a maximum absolute value in the layer and then decay to zero at
the boundary layer edge. This leads to the growth of longitudinal vortices
with their axes near the point of inflection, and the most noticeable are
those that are aligned with axes the have profiles with zero net crossflow
velocity at the point of inflection. This behavior is shown as the circles in
Fig. 11.9. Such longitudinal vortices are prominent features in visualizations

The spanwise spread of transition can also occur from streamwise corners,

in Chapter 6. The angle of the spread is about the same as that from turbulent spots, that is, about 11 deg in low-speed flows.
Supersonic flows are strongly unstable on swept wings. Scott-Wilson
and Capps (1954) suggest that compressibility has a destabilizing effect on
all 3D flows.
Suction has been found to stabilize a laminar 3D flow perhaps more
strongly than in 2D flows. This is because the suction reduces the magnitude of the crossflow velocity, as well as the boundary layer thickness.

11.4 Turbulent Three-Dimensional Boundary Layers

Copyright © 2011. American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics. All rights reserved.

11.4.1

Introduction

Recall that turbulence is always three-dimensional; that is, the fluctuating parts of the velocity components are all of the same order of magnitude,
even if the mean flow is two-dimensional (see Sec. 7.4). Thus, one might
conclude that there are no essential differences between 2D and 3D
turbulent boundary layer flows. But that is incorrect, as evidenced by the
much poorer state of the comparisons of predictions with experiments for
3D cases, as compared with 2D cases.
The first thing to consider in examining turbulent 3D boundary layers
is the occurrence of a class of secondary flows that happen only in turbulent flows. These are shear-driven secondary flows because the Reynolds
stresses create them. The simplest practical example is the straight rectangular duct with thin boundary layers (that is, the flow is not fully
developed), where gradients in the Reynolds stresses near the corners
drive the secondary flow (see Fig. 8.19). This situation creates a very
severe test for turbulence models. However, ducts are seldom straight in
practice, and the pressure-driven secondary flows in curved ducts usually
predominate.
A useful result concerning pressure-driven secondary flows in the outer
part of a 3D boundary layer was deduced by Bradshaw (1987), assuming
inviscid flow. Consider an initially 2D flow that encounters a spanwise
pressure gradient leading to a turn to the right and thus a 3D flow, as shown
in Fig. 11.10a. By Bernoulli’s equation, the velocity field is

Thus, a fluid element originally along AB in Fig. 11.10a will be convected
and turned after a time dt to be located along CD. The difference in the arc
lengths AC and BD is simply dt times the difference in velocity on the two
streamlines, which is proportional to minus the difference in the radii of the
arcs, by Eq. (11.42). So the angle between AB and CD is the same as the
turning angle a. In an inviscid flow, the vorticity vector is locked to a fluid
element; therefore, it turns as depicted in Fig. 11.10b. There is then a component PQ in the original flow direction, and a component PR twice as large
as PQ in the new flow direction, that is, perpendicular to CR. Finally, we see
that the angle between the vorticity vector and the velocity vector changes
by twice as much as the direction of flow. The crossflow component of the
vorticity vector is approximately 2'U/'y, and the streamwise component is
'W/'y. Thus, one can make a polar plot of W vs U, as illustrated in Fig.
11.11, and find that the slope, dW/dU, in the outermost portion is ('W/'y)/
('U/'y), or minus twice the angle of deflection of the velocity vector. This
formula, dW/dU 5 22α, known as the Squire-Winter-Hawthorn (SWH) formula, agrees very well with experiment, and it forms the basis of assumptions regarding velocity profile shapes that we will see later.

depicted in Fig. 11.12. We mentioned this before in Sec. 7.3.4, where the fact

crossflow component of the shear equal to m('W/'y). In a turbulent flow, the

are needed. The foregoing discussion shows that these components are not
necessarily equal, that is, the eddy viscosity is not, in general, isotropic.
With this brief orientation to the subject, we now proceed to a more
general discussion of 3D turbulent boundary layer flows. The practice is
the same as earlier in this book. First, representative mean flow data are
presented. This is followed by a presentation of turbulence data. Next, we
have a description of turbulence models for 3D flows. Finally, comparisons
of predictions with experiments are given, including both integral and differential methods. A great portion of the experimental data and computational results available is for the case of the so-called infinite swept wing
(see Sec. 11.2.2), so much of the discussion is restricted to that special case.

11.4.4

Integral Analyses

Integral analyses have remained competitive for turbulent 3D flows,
while for 2D flows they are now little used. The situation for turbulent 2D
cases is a little hard to understand because modern integral methods
perform about as well as the best differential methods in 2D at a fraction of
the cost. The reason for the continued use of integral methods in turbulent
3D cases may well be the higher cost of differential methods.
In a Eurovisc Workshop in 1982, calculations were compared with
experiment for a number of test cases, and several integral methods were
considered. The results are discussed in Van Den Berg et al. (1988). Recently,
the integral method of Moses (see Sec. 7.7) has been extended to 3D flows
by Caille and Schetz (1992). Two of the test cases studied at the Eurovisc
Workshop are experiments from Van Den Berg and Elsenaar (1972) and
Müller and Krause (1979). The first of these is a close simulation of an infinite swept wing, so the flow does not vary in the spanwise direction. That
should be a comparatively easy case. The second configuration is superficially similar, but the flow does vary in the spanwise direction, thus providing a more stringent test of analyses. These two test cases will be used here
to illustrate the quality of the predictions of the various methods.
The method of Smith (1972) uses power law streamwise velocity profiles

modeled with a differential equation accounting for changes in the structure

methods that utilize only a single strip (see Sec. 7.7).
The Cousteix (1974) method depends on functions obtained by solving
the differential equations of motion, assuming local similarity. Turbulence is
modeled with a mixing length formula extended to 3D, including anisotropy.
The similarity solutions provide relations among the integral thicknesses,
a skin friction law, and the entrainment velocity.
The method of Cross (1979) employs velocity profiles that are a generalization of the Coles 2D profile. This also leads to a skin friction law.
Finally, entrainment is modeled with an algebraic relation.
The integral method of Caille and Schetz (1992) aims to eliminate the
need for a skin friction law as input, in the same way that Moses accomplished that goal for 2D cases. Integral equations are written for two control
volumes, one encompassing the whole boundary layer, as usual, and the
second covering the region from the wall up through a fraction (about 35%)
of the boundary layer thickness. With this method, one needs velocity profile
shapes and a model for turbulent shear at the outer boundary of the inner
strip, that is, y L 0.35d. The velocity profiles are constructed using a generalization of the Moses 2D expression for the streamwise velocity,

no agreement in the literature as to a universal value. Some workers report
values less than unity and others values greater than unity. Only an outer
region model is required because the outer edge of the inner strip is in the
outer region ( y/d L 0.35).

The use of wall functions in 3D is more problematical than in 2D
because the required 3D wall law is not as well founded. The inner integral
momentum procedure of Caille and Schetz (1991) is more soundly based.
There is a relative paucity of work with higher-order turbulence models
for 3D boundary layer flows. Bradshaw (1971) extended his 2D TKE model
to 3D, and a comparison of predictions with the infinite swept wing
experiment of Bradshaw and Terrell (1969) is given in Fig. 11.33, along with
predictions from the Cebeci eddy viscosity model. No advantage can be
seen for the TKE model. The Johnson-King model (see Sec. 7.10) has been
extended to 3D (see Abid, 1988), and some workers report better results
than the Baldwin-Lomax and Cebeci-Smith models for finite wings with
strong pressure gradients.

11.5 Three-Dimensional Turbulent Jets
11.5.1

Introduction

The practical interest in three-dimensional jets stems from their frequent application as a mixing augmentation scheme. In the simplest view,
mixing is increased because the peripheral area around a 3D jet is increased,
compared with a 2D (for example, round) jet with the same fluid exhaust
rate. But there is more to it than that, as the turbulent structure in the jet
can also be altered. This alteration has been the subject of a number of
studies, with those of Schadow and his coworkers (for example, Ho and
Gutmark, 1987) being perhaps the best known.

11.5.2

Experimental Data

12.1

Numerical Solution Methods

H

igh-performance computing provides an opportunity to
develop generalized computational methods for fluid
dynamics. Modern computational fluid dynamics (CFD)
methods are based on solving the full conservation law equation set
without the boundary layer approximation, which allows one to
address problems that include separating flows, shock–boundary
layer interactions, complicated geometries, and other challenges.
Because of these advantages, CFD has emerged into a multidisciplinary subject involving fluid dynamics and computer science, where
multisemester graduate course sequences are required to fully appreciate the subject. The goal for this chapter is to provide an introduction to CFD for high-Reynolds-number viscous flow problems. For
more complete descriptions, see the comprehensive texts by Anderson
et al. (1984), Fletcher (1988), Hirsch (2007), and Hoffman and Chiang
(1995).
To demonstrate the advantage of Navier-Stokes numerical simulations, consider the hypersonic viscous interaction problem described
in Chapter 5, where boundary layer similarity and CFD solutions are
compared in Fig. 12.1 for Mach 6 flow over a flat plate. As indicated
in Fig. 12.1a, the boundary thicknesses differ by approximately 30%
between the two solutions. This is the expected result because the
similarity solution, which assumes parallel flow, does not account for

the boundary layer displacement effects. Conversely, the numerical NavierStokes solution naturally captures the viscous interaction, boundary-layerinduced shock wave, and subsequent pressure gradient (Fig. 12.1b). This
simple example demonstrates the utility of computational methods for the
Navier-Stokes equations.
Formally, as described in Chapter 1, the Navier-Stokes equations describe
conservation of momentum in differential form for Newtonian flows.
However, the modern meaning of the term Navier-Stokes equations has been
expanded to include all of the continuum flow conservation law equations.
Continuum and particle flow problems are categorized with the Knudsen
number, which is the ratio of the mean free path between molecular collisions

Schetz, Joseph A., and Rodney D.W. Bowersox. Boundary Layer Analysis, American Institute of Aeronautics and
Astronautics, 2011. ProQuest Ebook Central, http://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/delft/detail.action?docID=3111690.
Created from delft on 2026-09-28 12:41:25.

02/06/11 9:31 PM

Copyright © 2011. American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics. All rights reserved.

CHAPTER 12

Navier-Stokes Computational Fluid Dynamics

585

to the length scale of the problem. The Navier-Stokes equations are valid for
Knudsen numbers as high as order 0.1. However, the no-slip boundary condition (see Chapter 2) only holds for values less than order 0.01. The NavierStokes equation set can be quite general, where for reacting flows it may
include a conservation of mass equation for each species and a conservation
of energy equation for each internal degree of freedom. For this chapter,
we shall restrict the description to nonreacting, thermally and calorically
perfect gases. For more general reacting flow, the reader is referred to Walters
et al. (1992).
CFD methods fall into three basic categories: finite difference, finite
element, and finite volume methods. All three methods have been developed for three-dimensional problems. The basic idea behind all three
methods is that the flow domain be discretized into a very large number
of cells to which the governing equations are approximated. We are then
left with an algebraic system of equations for the flow properties at discrete locations within the flow. Modern simulations are approaching 109
cells. The numerical algorithms are designed to provide unique solutions to the governing equations that satisfy the boundary conditions of
the problem.
Finite difference formulations are based on using Taylor series expansions to replace differentials with finite differences on a mesh within the
domain; see Chapter 4. The order of accuracy of the numerical scheme is
the order of the leading term truncated in the Taylor series, which depends
on the number and arrangement of the grid points used, called the stencil,
to build the finite difference formulation. Finite difference methods are
usually applied to structured, or prismatic, grids; see Fig. 12.2a. For complicated three-dimensional geometries, the generation of the intricate grids
can be a daunting but very important part of the solution. One of the key
challenges with finite difference methods is properly capturing shock
waves. The difficulty lies in the fact that the differential form of the conservation law equations requires continuous flow properties. As described in
Chapter 5, under continuum conditions, shock waves are very thin, on the
order of three to five mean free paths. Hence, shock waves are treated
numerically as discontinuities, which is the case with the Rankine-Hugoniot shock relations. These discontinuities violate the differential form of
the equations. Finite element methods are based on approximating the
flow variables over the discretized elements with interpolation functions
and then minimizing errors; see Chapter 4.
The primary focus of this chapter is finite volume methods because
they have emerged into the popular choice for a wide range of fluid
dynamic problems. Finite volume methods discretize the integral forms of
the conservation law equations. Thus, they naturally capture shock waves

Astronautics, 2011. ProQuest Ebook Central, http://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/delft/detail.action?docID=3111690.

as the integral equations reduce to the Rankine-Hugoniot jump relations
in the limit of vanishing small volumes. A second advantage of the finite
volume method is the readiness in which irregular or unstructured meshes
are handled. An example of an unstructured grid is shown in Fig. 12.2b.
The advantages of unstructured meshes are the ability to adapt to complex
geometries and to cluster points in high-gradient regions. The disadvantage is that the resulting numerical matrices that require inversion are not
diagonally banded. This eliminates many of the approximate inversion
methods that have proven to be numerically efficient for structured
meshes. Finite volume methods are applicable to both structured and
unstructured grids.

Integral Form of the Navier-Stokes Equations

The integral equations of fluid motion for a gas that satisfies the
continuum assumption stem directly from the conservation law principles as applied to a fixed system of fluid particles. The statements are
as follows:
• Conservation of mass: The time rate of change of mass is equal to zero.
• Conservation of momentum: The time rate of change of momentum is
equal to the net forces acting on system of particles.
• Conservation of energy: The time rate of change of the energy is equal
to the rate of heat gained by the system plus the rate of work done on
the system by the force acting on the system.
Mathematically, we cast these conservation statements as follows:

(12.1)

An important feature of Eq. (12.1) is that it applies to a fixed system of fluid
particles. To apply the conservation laws in the form of Eq. (12.1), we must
track all of the individual fluid particles that make up our system; this is
called the Lagrangian approach. The more practical approach is to fix a
volume in space and track the particles as they pass through the volume;
this is called the Eulerian approach. A key point here is that the conservation laws, as stated in Eq. (12.1), do not directly apply to a fixed volume in
space. Before moving on to the conservation law equations, it is important
to note that e0 is the total energy, which is the sum of the internal and kinetic energies (e + ½V 2), and for reacting systems the internal energy e
includes both the sensible, or temperature-dependent, energy and the heat
of formation.

The time-dependent Navier-Stokes equations are, in general, mixed hyperbolic and parabolic in form. In the inviscid region of the flow, the equations are
hyperbolic, and in the viscous layers, the equations are parabolic. The steadystate Navier-Stokes equations are hyperbolic in the inviscid regions and elliptic
in the viscous regions. Many modern computational flow solvers achieve
steady-state solutions by marching the unsteady form of the equations in time
until the solution becomes numerically independent of time.

differential equations (for example, see Atkinson et al., 2009). As described

involve large-scale matrix inversion. However, they suffer from stability
constraints, which can be severe for high-Reynolds-number problems with
thin viscous regions. Implicit methods are usually unconditionally stable.

intensive.

As discussed in Chapter 4, explicit methods result in simple and relatively fast numerical algorithms. However, explicit algorithms are
subject to numerical stability constraints. A stable numerical scheme is
one in which perturbations, such as numerical round off, are inherently
damped as the solution progresses. If the perturbations grow, the
scheme is called unstable. The Navier-Stokes equations do not permit
closed-form stability analyses. However, extensive von Neumann and
matrix stability studies have been performed on model equations and
linearized forms of the Euler equations, which provide guidance for
empirical stability studies. A general rule of thumb for explicit methods
is that the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) number (Courant et al.,
1928) is less than order unity. Related empirical stability constraints are
often used for viscous flow, such as (Tannehill et al., 1975)

12.5.3

Numerical Dissipation and Artificial
Viscosity

Another important inference from the modified equations is the form
of the leading truncated spatial derivative on the right-hand side. The
leading derivatives for the first-order schemes in Eqs. (12.22) and (12.23)
are even derivatives of the form 1/2 Dx 3 '2 1 f 2 fn 2 pn,m/'x 2 4 , which resembles
a viscous flux, for example, m'2u/'y 2. Numerical solutions using first-order
schemes have proven to be overly dissipative, where they smooth gradients
over many grid cells.
For the central difference scheme in Eq. (12.15), the leading term is a
third-order derivative [Eq. (12.18)]. For this scheme, very little numerical
dissipation is present. The difficulty with this result is reduced stability
and oscillations near strong gradients, for example, shock waves. To overcome this limitation, additional terms are added to the formulation to
increase stability and eliminate spurious oscillations near shock waves.
Numerous approaches have been proposed in the literature (for example,
Jameson et al., 1981; Jameson, 1992; Kawai and Lele, 2007). These techniques have proven effective at minimizing both dispersion and diffusion
of the shock wave flows. Cook and Cabot (2004) introduced artificial
dynamic and bulk viscosities that are added to the molecular viscosity to
dampen high-wave-number oscillations. In their formulation, the viscosities are given by
mA 5 AmrDr12 0 =rS 0 ,

lA 5 Al rDr12 0 =rS 0

where mA and lA are the artificial dynamic and bulk viscosities,
A( ) are user-defined constants, D is the local grid spacing, S is the magnitude of the strain rate tensor, r controls the wave number bias,
and the overbar denotes a Gaussian filter. Extensions of this method for
high-order differencing are described in Kawai and Lele (2007).
The artificial dissipation method of Jameson et al. (1981) is used in the
CNSA applet.

approach is similar, with the additional constraint that the split flux vector
be a smooth function of Mach number. Roe’s (1981) flux differencing splitting scheme is based on using an approximate solution to the Riemann
problem. This method, with the Harten (1984) entropy correction, is one of
the most used methods.

Limiters and Total Variation Diminishing
Schemes

Gudanov’s (1954) theorem states that for linear finite difference models,
first-order schemes are required to ensure monotone solutions to partial
differential equations. Higher-order schemes are required to capture flow
gradients such as boundary layers and secondary flow. However, near discontinuities or very high gradient regions, high-order schemes can overshoot and produced nonphysical oscillations. Limiters are introduced to
overcome this problem. There are a number of popular limiters in use; for
example, see van Albada et al. (1982). The role of the limiter is to lower the
order of the scheme to first order near the discontinuity.
The discrete total variation (TV) is defined as
`

TV 1 Q p 2 5 a 0 Q pn11 2 Q pn 0

Copyright © 2011. American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics. All rights reserved.

2`

The idea behind the total variation diminishing (TVD) schemes is that for
the solution to remain nonoscillatory, the total variation must remain the
same or decrease as the solution proceeds; that is, TV 1 Q p11 2 ⱕ TV 1 Q p 2
(Harten, 1983). TVD schemes are limited to smoothly varying meshes.
Essentially nonoscillatory (ENO) schemes are polynomial reconstructions
designed to obtain higher-order accuracy on general meshes. ENO schemes
use the smoothest stencil among several candidates to approximate the
fluxes at cell boundaries to achieve high-order accuracy and avoid spurious
oscillations. For weighted ENO (WENO) schemes, a weighted combination
of all candidate stencils is used. Each of the candidate stencils is assigned a
weight that determines the contribution of this stencil to the final approximation of the numerical flux. WENO schemes also remove the logical
statements that appear in the ENO stencil choosing step. Thus, WENO
schemes are significantly faster. For more details on ENO and WENO
schemes, see Harten et al. (1986) and G.-S. Jiang and Shu (1996).

12.5.6

Boundary Conditions

The boundary conditions are an essential part of generating accurate
solutions. Specification of the boundary value is called a Dirichlet boundary condition, and specification of a gradient at the boundary is called a
Neumann condition. Many problems are mixed, where some boundary
values are set by Dirichlet conditions and the others by Neumann conditions. On solid surfaces, we have the no-slip boundary conditions described
in Chapter 1. Specifically, the velocity of the gas is equal to the velocity of
the solid surface at the solid surface. Similarly, either the temperature of the

the heat transfer is set to zero. For steady supersonic flows, the inflow condition is set, and for boundaries where the flow exits the domain, extrapolation is used. An advantage of supersonic flows is that the domain of
dependence and range of influence are restricted by the characteristic
directions in the flow. Therefore, the solution domains can be minimized
without adversely affecting the accuracy of the solution. Subsonic flows, on
the other hand, typically require very large grids to minimize the influence
of the boundary on the solutions. The grids shown in Fig. 12.3 are typical
of low-speed airfoil simulations, where the domain extends on the order of
10 chord lengths in all directions. Even with grids that extend order 10
chord lengths, vorticity corrections are required. To eliminate the need for
corrections, the grid may have to extend order 100 chord lengths. For more
details on the various boundary conditions, refer to the sources mentioned
in Sec. 12.1.

Copyright © 2011. American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics. All rights reserved.

12.5.7 Thin-Layer and Parabolized Navier-Stokes
Equations
For some problems, such as airfoils, the viscous derivatives in the
streamwise (j) direction are much smaller than those in the normal (h)
direction. If we neglect the streamwise derivatives, the system is significantly simplified. The resulting equations are called the thin-layer NavierStokes equations. For subsonic problems, the main advantage of the
thin-layer equations is the elimination of off-diagonal terms in the resulting linear system, which speeds up the numerical convergence. For supersonic flows, the reduced equations are parabolic. The advantage of the
parabolized Navier-Stokes equations is the applicability of space marching
to solve the problem. This results in considerable time savings. For viscous
flows with a subsonic region within the boundary layer, the pressure terms
in f and g are multiplied by the Vigneron et al. (1978) factor, which is given
by gM 2j / 3 1 1 1 g 2 1 2 M 2j 4 . This factor ensures that the eigenvalues of the
Jacobians are positive. For more details on parabolized flow solvers, refer to
the sources mentioned in Sec. 12.1.

12.6 Turbulent Flows

Numerical simulation of turbulent flows falls into the three basic
categories: 1) direct numerical simulation (DNS), 2) partially resolved
methods, for example, large eddy simulations (LES) and detached eddy
simulations (DES), and 3) Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS). For
both DNS and partially resolved methods, higher-order differencing is

12.7

Grid Generation

Grid generation is a critical aspect of producing accurate numerical
simulation results. As described in Sec. 12.1, grids fall into two basic categories, structured and unstructured. The choice is often dictated by the
problem at hand. Structured grids offer the advantage that the resulting
matrices that require inversion [for example, Eq. (12.30)] are banded, and
this enables the use of rapid, approximate inversion methods. The disadvantage is the difficulty in adapting to complex configurations. However,

clustering, where the fine-grid results interface with the surrounding outer
grid through interpolation. Unstructured grids are particularly well suited
for complex geometries and adaptive algorithms. Shown in Fig. 12.5 is an
example of a grid clustered about a hypersonic boundary layer trip element,
where the trip height is on the order of the boundary layer thickness. Adaptive gridding techniques automatically adjust the clustering of grid points
in high-gradient regions during the mesh refinement.
The rule of thumb for turbulence calculations is that the first grid cell
should be located near y1 5 1. Hence, grid stretching is required (see
Chapter 7), and nominally, 100 grid points should span the boundary layer.
For laminar flows, 20–50 grid points nearly evenly distributed across a
boundary layer are typically considered acceptable. Demonstrating grid
independence is required practice if numerical results are to be trusted. An
accepted manner to demonstrate grid independence is to run the problem
on successively finer meshes until the difference between solutions is
within an acceptable tolerance.

12.8

Comments for Producing Accurate Solutions

The purpose of this chapter is to introduce modern finite volume CFD
methods. We end with advice on attaining the highest possible accuracy
available.
The first step in producing an accurate numerical result is to have an a
priori understanding of the physical processes so that appropriate physical
and numerical models can be selected. The first 11 chapters of this text
Schetz, Joseph A., and Rodney D.W. Bowersox. Boundary Layer Analysis, American Institute of Aeronautics and
Astronautics, 2011. ProQuest Ebook Central, http://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/delft/detail.action?docID=3111690.
Created from delft on 2026-09-28 12:41:25.

SCHETZ Chapter_12.indd 604

02/06/11 9:31 PM

CHAPTER 12

Navier-Stokes Computational Fluid Dynamics

605

Copyright © 2011. American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics. All rights reserved.

provide the necessary background to make informed choices. The impact of
these choices can be important in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. For
example, the solution procedure for supersonic flow over a sharp, thin, flat
wing will be significantly different than that used for incompressible flow
over a sphere. For the former case, the flow is supersonic in the flow direction and hence spatially hyperbolic. Thus, upwind, or backward, differencing is appropriate. The state of the boundary layer (laminar, turbulent, or
transitional) and hence the viscous model will depend on the expected
Reynolds numbers. For most current simulations, this selection is part of
the problem setup. Last, for this case, separation is unlikely. Hence, a very
efficient space marching scheme would be appropriate. For the latter subsonic sphere case, the flow is elliptic. Thus, central differencing is appropriate. The state of the boundary layer on the sphere also needs to be specified.
However, for this case, separation is likely, and if the flow is turbulent, the
turbulence model will have to be appropriate for this class of flow.
The second step in producing credible numerical results is demonstrating convergence, both grid (see Sec. 12.7) and numerical. For steady-state
problems, we integrate Eq. (12.8) until the residual is reduced to the desired
tolerance. A Euclidean norm is often used, where the residual is typically
reduced by five to six orders of magnitude. However, reducing the residual
below a tolerance may not lead to a fully converged solution. It is often
necessary to continue iterating beyond the tolerance to allow the skin friction and heat transfer to level out to the steady value. This step may double
or even triple the number of iterations.
The F/A-18 full aircraft simulation of Morton et al. (2004) is an excellent
example of modern simulation capabilities. The grid and an example flow
visualization result are given in Fig. 12.6. For these simulations, cell-centered
finite volume Navier-Stokes solutions were performed on unstructured grids
with approximately 3.9 million cells using the commercial code Cobalt
(Cobalt Solutions, LLC). Time-accurate simulations were performed using a
point-implicit scheme with Newton subiterations; 10,000 iterations were
accomplished to provide a time-accurate solution. A second-order, exact
Riemann solver, similar in function to Roe’s scheme, was used for the spatial
discretization. The physical model was thermally and calorically perfect air,
and the turbulence was simulated using a DES model with Spalart-Allmaras
(SA) Reynolds averaging for attached wall boundary layers. The purpose of
the simulation was to examine the effects of leading-edge-extensiongenerated large-scale vortices, and the breakdown thereof, on tail buffeting.
Currently, there are a number of available commercial finite volume
Navier-Stokes software and grid generation packages that have been
developed for complex geometries. These are often relatively straight
forward to use because they interface with the user through graphical user
interfaces (GUIs).
